claims.text: During sliding in air at 600–800 °C, the FeNiCrCoCu coating will form an in situ tribo-oxide film.
The tribo-oxide film will be thin, continuous, and adherent.
The tribo-oxide film will be enriched in Cu and Cr oxides.
Oxide-film formation will be minimal or absent during otherwise equivalent sliding in inert argon.
High-temperature exposure in an oxidizing environment causes the tribo-oxide film to form rapidly.
The tribo-oxide film reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
The tribo-oxide film acts as both a solid lubricant and a protective barrier.
Relative to the argon baseline, sliding in air will reduce the coating's wear rate or wear volume.
Relative to the argon baseline, sliding in air will reduce the friction coefficient.
Relative to the argon baseline, sliding in air will increase surface microhardness.
Tribo-oxide formation changes microscopic deformation from localized severe plasticity to more homogeneous, distributed deformation.
The oxide film modifies the dominant deformation mechanism from dislocation-mediated plasticity to less localized plastic deformation.
The predicted oxide-mediated improvements apply primarily within the 600–800 °C sliding regime.
Overly rapid oxidation can cause excessive spallation and invalidate the proposed protective mechanism.
Failure to form a significant adherent oxide film, or absence of the predicted wear and deformation improvements, would falsify the hypothesis.
